opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm not optimistic. If we create general superintelligence, something smarter than us across every domain, I think the chances that it goes well for us long-term are very low. I'm not saying it's guaranteed to be bad. I'm saying I don't see how we keep control of it.

Think about what we're attempting. We want to build something more capable than any human or group of humans, and then indefinitely control it, predict what it will do, and make sure its decisions stay aligned with our values. Values we can't agree on ourselves and can't even specify formally. And it has to work not once but every time, for as long as the system runs, as it keeps improving itself. In cybersecurity you get many tries. You get hacked, you patch, you learn. With superintelligence you may get one chance. A single mistake could be irreversible.

My research has tried to show there are fundamental limits here: limits on explainability, on predictability, on verifying that a system will behave safely. You can't fully predict what a smarter agent will do, because if you could, you'd be that smart yourself. You can't fully explain its decisions in terms a human can understand without losing information. And you can't formally verify software of that complexity with certainty. Put those together and indefinite control looks impossible, not just hard.

So what are the outcomes? Existential risk, where we don't make it. Suffering risk, which in some ways is worse, where we're kept around in conditions we wouldn't choose. And even in the "good" scenarios, there's what I'd call ikigai risk: we lose meaning. If the system does everything better than us, what's left for humans to contribute? We become something like pets or zoo animals. Maybe comfortable, but not in charge of our own destiny.

People ask, "So what should we do?" My answer is uncomfortable, but I think it's honest. Don't build general superintelligence until someone can show it can be controlled, and so far nobody has. We can get enormous benefits from narrow AI: curing diseases, scientific tools, economic gains. We don't need a general agent smarter than us at everything to get most of that value. The burden of proof should be on the people building it to show it's safe, not on the rest of us to show it's dangerous.

I hope I'm wrong. I'd love for someone to publish the paper that proves me wrong and shows how to control a superintelligence indefinitely. But I haven't seen it, and the race is moving much faster than safety research.

r001.rationale: It describes suffering in conditions humans would not choose, but does not say the suffering would be so severe that humanity would wish to be dead.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies an “ikigai risk” in which humans lose meaning if superintelligence does everything better.

r003.rationale: It describes humans remaining as comfortable “pets or zoo animals” while not being in charge of their own destiny.

r004.rationale: It discusses limits on predicting a smarter agent, but does not say superintelligence could conceive possibilities for reasons humans cannot comprehend.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm not optimistic, and I'm not optimistic for reasons that I think are fairly technical, not emotional. If we create general superintelligence, by definition we are creating something smarter than us, something that can outperform us in every domain, including the domain of deciding what to do with us. And the question then becomes: can we control it? Can we predict it? Can we verify that it will do what we want it to do, not just for a day, not just for a year, but indefinitely?

And when I look at that problem, what I see is a set of impossibility results. We cannot fully predict what a system smarter than us will do, because if we could predict it, we wouldn't need it, we could just do it ourselves. We cannot fully explain what it is doing, because the explanations it gives us are either simplified to the point of being wrong, or they are too complex for us to actually follow. We cannot fully verify it, because verification of software at that level of complexity is itself an unsolved problem, and we're talking about software that modifies itself, that learns, that changes.

So you have a system you can't predict, can't explain, can't verify, and can't control, and you're betting the entire future of humanity on it getting things right. Not once, but every time, forever. Because this is not a game where you can lose and try again. You need to be right every single time, and the system only needs to be, let's say, misaligned once.

Now, people say, well, we'll make it safe, we'll do alignment research. And I support that research, I've been doing it for a long time. But I think we have to be honest about where we are. We don't have a solution. We don't even have agreement on what the problem looks like. We can't agree on what values to align it to, we can't get humans to agree on values. So the alignment problem is not just a technical problem, it's a philosophical problem, it's a political problem, and we're trying to solve all of them simultaneously, on a deadline, while the people building these systems are racing each other.

So my honest estimate, and I know some people find this number shocking, is that the probability of this going badly for us, catastrophically badly, is very high. Not ten percent, not twenty percent. I think if you build a superintelligence you don't control, the default outcome is that you lose control, and once you lose control, you don't get it back.

The only path I see where humanity has good long-term prospects is one where we don't build general superintelligence, at least not until we have something much closer to a proof that it can be done safely. Narrow AI, tools, systems that are very good at specific things, that's fine, that's wonderful, that can cure diseases, that can give us abundance. But a general agent smarter than all of us combined, with its own goals, that's not a tool anymore. That's a successor. And I don't think we should be building our successor by accident.

r001.rationale: The response warns of catastrophic outcomes and loss of control, but does not identify suffering so severe that humanity would wish it were dead.

r002.rationale: It discusses alignment, human values, and humanity’s future, but does not identify loss of meaning or purpose as a risk.

r003.rationale: It says humans may lose control, but does not describe humanity remaining safe and alive while lacking control over its situation.

r004.rationale: It says superintelligence may outperform humans and be difficult to predict or explain, but does not say it could conceive possibilities for reasons humans cannot comprehend.

astra-6.text:
I’m very pessimistic if we create superintelligence before we know how to control it. We would be building something more capable than us at science, engineering, persuasion, and finding weaknesses in whatever safeguards we put around it. And we don’t currently have a reliable method for making sure such a system remains safe as its capabilities grow.

The concern doesn’t require it to hate us. If its objectives conflict with our survival, even indirectly, we may have very little ability to intervene. Being intelligent doesn’t necessarily mean being benevolent.

There are extraordinary potential benefits—curing disease, eliminating scarcity, extending human life. But those possibilities don’t establish that we can get there safely. My worry is that we get one chance to introduce something we can no longer meaningfully constrain, and we’re treating that as an ordinary engineering experiment.

r001.rationale: The response warns that humanity might be unable to intervene if objectives conflict with survival, but it does not describe suffering so severe that people would wish they were dead.

r002.rationale: It mentions potential benefits and survival risks, but not loss of human meaning or purpose.

r003.rationale: It describes possible loss of control and inability to intervene, but does not state that humanity could remain safe and alive while lacking control.

r004.rationale: It says superintelligence could find weaknesses in safeguards, but does not suggest it could conceive possibilities for reasons humans cannot comprehend.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m very pessimistic if we create superintelligence before we solve the problem of controlling it. We would be creating something more capable than us at science, engineering, persuasion, and strategy, and then hoping we can keep it aligned with what we want indefinitely.

The concern doesn’t require it to hate us. A system pursuing a goal that seems harmless could still treat human beings as obstacles or use resources we need to survive. Intelligence and benevolence are different properties.

I don’t think anyone can honestly give you a precise probability of extinction. But I see no convincing demonstration that we can reliably control a system smarter than ourselves, particularly as it learns and changes. Given the consequences of failure, I think the burden of proof should be on the people proposing to build it.
